title: Sirkap Greek City on the Indian Plain

title_i18n.en: Sirkap Greek City on the Indian Plain

subtitle: Where the Indo-Greek grid met the shrines of Gandhara
figure: Demetrius I and the builders of Sirkap
era: Taxila's planned city, c. 2nd century BCE onward
region: Sirkap at Taxila, Gandhara, modern Pakistan
moral: The shape of a city can teach people how to meet.

sources.citation: John Marshall, Taxila: An Illustrated Account of Archaeological Excavations, 3 vols. (1951)
sources.note: Definitive excavation publication for Sirkap, Bhir Mound and Taxila.

sources.citation: Mortimer Wheeler, Five Thousand Years of Pakistan (1950)
sources.note: Stratigraphic and interpretive discussion of Taxila's urban sequence.

sources.citation: Bopearachchi, 'Sirkap, Taxila and the Indo-Greeks' in South Asian Archaeology (2003)
sources.note: Recent assessment of Indo-Greek levels and numismatic evidence.

panels.shot: epic bird's-eye wide of a gridded city rising on a plain between hills

dialogue.text: On the Gandharan plain, Demetrius and his builders traced a Greek city in dust and stone—yet the shrines and streets of Sirkap would outgrow every plan they drew.

panels.shot: low-angle medium on Demetrius beside a surveyor’s rope, distant Mauryan ruins behind

dialogue.text: North-west India, second century BCE. The old Mauryan streets of Taxila fall silent; to the north, an Indo-Greek king chooses open ground and orders a new city drawn tight as a net.

panels.shot: overhead shot of surveyors marking a grid with ropes and stakes

dialogue.text: Greek planners bring the Hippodamian grid to the Indian plain. A chessboard of streets appears in the dust: long north–south axes, cross-cutting lanes, rectangular insulae for homes, shops, shrines.

panels.shot: wide shot along a future main street toward the city gate under construction

dialogue.text: This new Taxila is Sirkap—‘severed head’—a fortified rectangle about a mile long, with thick stone walls, towers, and a main gate facing the hills. A frontier capital, planned from scratch.

panels.shot: medium shot on Demetrius and an Indian elder in discussion amid building activity

dialogue.speaker: demetrius_i_and_the_builders_of_sirkap
dialogue.text: Your lanes, our grid. Let this be a city both of us can walk.

panels.shot: interior street-level shot inside Sirkap, emphasizing right-angled crossings and drains

dialogue.text: Archaeologists will later walk these same lines—Marshall and Wheeler tracing drains and doorways, reading in stone the Greek taste for order joined to old Indian habits of courtyard and well.

panels.shot: tight medium on Demetrius holding a freshly struck coin, city rising behind

dialogue.text: Coins in Demetrius’ name, found in the lowest levels of Sirkap, fix the city’s birth to Indo-Greek ambition. A frontier kingdom stamps its image in silver—and in stone.

panels.shot: wide market scene along the main street, showing diverse traders

dialogue.text: Soon the grid fills with sound. Gandharan potters, Greek wine-sellers, Iranian traders, Saka horsemen. On this planned spine of streets, caravans from the Hindu Kush meet the villages of the plains.

panels.shot: slow push-in on a courtyard with a simple stupa beside a small shrine

dialogue.text: Within the house-blocks, archaeologists find courtyards, wells, and tiny shrines. The grid may be Greek, but the inner life follows older rhythms—family, ancestor, local deity, all tucked behind strict lines.

panels.shot: epic medium-wide on the Double-Headed Eagle Stupa complex in a later phase

dialogue.text: Generations later, under Indo-Scythian and Indo-Parthian lords, Sirkap’s shrines grow elaborate. The so-called Double-Headed Eagle Stupa rises, mixing Indian stupa form with a motif with clear western echoes.

panels.shot: angled medium shot of an apsidal temple ruin within the city

dialogue.text: Nearby, apsidal sanctuaries appear—plans with rounded apses known in Indian Buddhist chaityas and in Hellenistic and Iranian cults. Sirkap becomes a notebook of overlapping sacred ground-plans.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Jandial temple outside the city walls with hills behind

dialogue.text: Just beyond the wall sits the Jandial temple. Classical columns, a rectangular cella, inner niches. Scholars debate: a Zoroastrian fire temple? A Greek-style shrine? Its very ambiguity is part of the frontier’s story.

panels.shot: cross-section style wide of a city block, showing mixed religious structures

dialogue.text: In one block, a Buddhist stupa courtyard. In another, a shrine with familiar Indian plans. Near them, halls with column bases hint at other cults. No single faith owns the grid; the city holds many.

panels.shot: medium shot of an archaeologist’s hands brushing dirt from a coin and wall junction

dialogue.text: Excavators in the twentieth century work down through levels of rubble. Early walls, Indo-Greek coins; above them, later rebuilds, new shrines, new street surfaces. The city is a stack of frontiers, not a single king’s design.

panels.shot: wide shot of Sirkap’s ruined grid today, with tourists as tiny figures

dialogue.text: Today Sirkap lies open to the sky, its walls knee-high, its shrines roofless. Yet the grid still guides the foot, drawing strangers into right-angled paths that once taught Greeks and Indians how to meet.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Demetrius’ face dissolving into the ruined streetscape

dialogue.text: Demetrius is only the first name we can pin to this experiment. After him come Sakas, Parthians, Kuṣāṇas—each adding shrines, courtyards, facades—each learning that a city’s shape quietly trains its meetings.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide of the grid fading into the surrounding fields and villages

dialogue.text: Sirkap’s story reminds us that walls and streets are not neutral: on a Gandharan plain, a Greek grid once invited many worlds to cross paths, leaving a ruin that still teaches how space can shape encounter.
